utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic also know as "Vlado".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Let me take advantage of these few seconds or minutes before the witness is brought in. First of all, I it may sound pedantic, but I wonder whether the Prosecutor could be so kind as to give us a list of witnesses according to the protective measures, because now we've been a given a list with the names of the various Prosecutors that are going to take the examination-in-chief, but we need a list of the protective measures to know -- if it is possible at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: The remaining witnesses for this week do not have protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: None of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's correct. For this week. We're not, of course, talking about the Court witness that will appear today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. She asked for the closed session. Thank you. I think Counsel Slokovic-Glumac was still cross-examining the witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, one of the accused has just advised me that they are not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the usher would -- yes, so the earphones probably should be changed. Thank you. Counsel Glumac

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (continued):

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours. We stopped yesterday when we were discussing the village of Miletici and your visit to that village. Can you please tell us what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived at the village and were directed to a particular house where we found that -- well, we entered the house and found a room that had been -- had been destroyed to a certain extent, and there was blood on the floor and on the walls.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the local population, the people who still remained in the village, tell you what had happened in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that a number of Mujahedin, and if I'm not mistaken, the number was five, had come to the village approximately three days prior to that event. If I remember correctly, it was the 16th of April when the reported murders had occurred, and that they harassed the villagers and basically stayed in that house. We were told that there were -- there were two brothers that lived in that house, and that they were Croatian fighters, and supposedly these Mujahedin were waiting for them to return from a frontline or from somewhere. I think I was told the frontline. We asked them -- oftentimes you can hear the term "Mujahedin" being used as a term for Muslims in general and so on. However, the woman that I spoke with told me that no, these were foreigners, these were definitely foreign Mujahedin, that that wasn't just a term.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In your report, the number of people killed is listed as five young Croats. Some of them had been tortured. Does this correspond with the facts that you were able to establish there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It is also mentioned here that 27 out of the 34 Croatian inhabitants of the village had fled in fear of those persons. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact numbers, but I remember that this was brought to the attention of British battalion and our attention, because the UNHCR was afraid that the rest of the villagers would leave, creating another humanitarian crisis, and the representative of the UNHCR believed that the situation could be controlled and that -- I believe that she was trying to convince British battalion to go protect the village, and so that she could return -- for some reason I have the number 27 of 37, but more than half of the village had left, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You established, without a shadow of doubt, that the victims were Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that the village was a Croatian village. I'm not sure if all of the inhabitants were Croat, but we were told it was a Croatian village and the victims were indeed all Croats, and also that -- I think that three of the five were not from the village but the two brothers were from that house. I think that they owned that house, or that was their family home. I'm not really sure about those details.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At the time when you visited that area, did you visit other Croatian villages from which Croats had fled? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the context of fact finding. We did travel around quite a bit, especially on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you visit Zenica? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we visited Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice any problems related to the status of Croats at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really. Not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In your report it is mentioned that arbitrary executions and harassment was perpetrated by the government forces, the BH army, that is, and that there was a risk of reprisals for ethnic cleansing carried out by Croats and Croatian forces against Croatian civilians in cities such as Zenica, and that that risk or that danger was very real.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Whereabouts in the report are you reading from, please, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Third section, "Conclusions", paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the reference -- the earlier reference to the five Croats, where is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is in section 2, paragraph 37, on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Referring to the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No. That's the section entitled "Arbitrary Executions by Government Forces in the Vitez Area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not referring to Ahmici itself but to the Vitez area, I think that should be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is the same time period and all the events were happening at the same time, so the Prosecutor is also trying to show us a broader picture and that's what we are trying to do right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But the reference in this paragraph, so I can follow it, appears to be to Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, do you remember this portion or you don't have any knowledge of this, relating to the problems in Zenica that were taking place from the 16th onward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many problems in that area at the time. It wasn't a clear situation. There were reported incidents throughout the valley, as well as many other parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But your mandate covered the whole of the Lasva Valley as far as I understood. You were supposed to submit a report on the human rights situation in the whole area, not just in Ahmici. You included Vitez, the surrounding area, you even noted down some problems in the Zenica area. So this was -- all of this was part of your mandate at the time. That's the reason why I'm asking you whether you carried out any other investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the two that I mentioned, plus you can see that we included other information that was related to us, to the best of our ability, what we had available at the time. There was also -- I'm not really sure which information was added by Mr. Mazowiecki himself and his staff in Geneva. We tried to cover the situation as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Colonel Stewart on those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember the 4th of May, that is before you went to Ahmici, did you talk to Colonel Stewart, you and Mr. Akhavan? That's before you left for Ahmici, when you found that house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have. I'm sure we talked in passing. We spoke on many occasions. I'm sure we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember were journalists with you on that occasion? As far as I understand, they went with you into the village, Andrew Hawke and Dan Damon from Sunday Times. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an occasion when the Colonel was having a meeting with the liaison staff from the two conflicting parties in a house. I think that was the ECMM liaison house, I'm not sure. There was a house that was out of the base that was used for liaison between the local authorities, and just a basic liaison house. We waited in front of that house to speak with the Colonel to see when we would be able to travel to Ahmici. I think that was our purpose for waiting. There were journalists that were in that meeting, then they were excluded from that meeting, they were outside and so on. I remember that they tried to interview us but we were not authorised to give interviews and we told them that we can't be interviewed at all, that we're here just to write a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. After your conversation with the victims that you had met in Zenica, did you supply Colonel Stewart with a list of names or mention some of the people that you talked to, that they claimed that some people had been perpetrators of the crimes in Ahmici? So did you give any names to Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so. We discussed at length with his officers, but I don't believe that we gave anything to British battalion. I'm not sure. It's possible that something was handed over, but I don't recollect any piece of paper. It was more of a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you write down some of the names that have been mentioned by the people from Ahmici, the refugees? Did you write down those names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names of the perpetrators or the names of the refugees, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you state that you did not give any names related to those events to Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you, in any way, go to Vitez in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, as a part of a patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what did you establish there? Did you go to Stari Vitez? Stari Vitez, that's the Muslim part of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was the first day, the first patrol that was for the benefit of the incoming battalion. That was pointed out to us. We stopped, I think very close to -- there seemed to be a division at some point, a couple of streets, and that -- and we stopped there and some things were pointed out to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice any fortifications around Stari Vitez, roadblocks, trenches, bunkers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- there were positions. There were positions on several roads. There were armed individuals in many areas, in Vitez and surrounding Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The presence -- you also noted the presence of the BH army soldiers. Can you give us the number of soldiers that you saw in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if I could. There were -- there were men with weapons at different points. There was one group of four at one place, there was another group of maybe two or three. If I had to estimate how many I saw in total, I probably would have seen as many as, I don't know, 30, maybe 40, but that's just an estimate, I never counted anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: While you were there and when you visited Stari Vitez, was there any sniper action out of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no hostilities at the time, but we were told -- I think when we drove very close to the town and so on, I think the tank commander at that point locked us down. It was an environment that wasn't safe, so we were in a locked tank rather than in something open where we could view.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So there was no sniper fire from that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not when we visited the area, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one more thing regarding the notes that you had with you yesterday, notes from which you read the names of persons which you assumed you had found in [redacted] house. Where did you get those notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those notes were left, I assume, in my office, and they were given to me by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The notes where you transcribed the contents of the statement from the tape of (redacted) and [redacted], so that's part of those notes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are the notes. Those are the notes of a combination of a transcription, translation and recollection that I put down on paper, as I said, to provide to any individuals who would be conducting a future investigation. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. This means that notes and the notes with the names of the victims, you got from the Prosecutor. So these are your notes that you received from the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're not two separate notes, they're one note. It's one document. I received a copy of this from the Prosecutor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Since the witness has confirmed and authenticated these notes, I don't know why the Defence has not been given a copy so that we see what this is all about. These notes, after all, can have a certain probative value. We think that the Prosecutor should have supplied us with a copy of the notes so that we can see what they are all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, it was -- these notes, as we have them, are not statements of any of the witnesses that have testified, because as this witness has indicated, these are his notes and his recollection of what transpired, and contain a sort of combination of his recollection and what he could get off the tapes of those two witnesses. So they're not statements, they certainly were never signed by the witnesses or reviewed by the witnesses. Nor, in our view, were these statements of this witnesses. They were simply his notes of what he recalled having transpired between him and these witnesses. So it appeared to us that this certainly did not fit into any category that required disclosure. They are useful as a diary, or any other document, might be useful to a witness to assist him in recollecting what he, in fact, remembered of these conversations, and that would be, I think, the real focus of his testimony here today, as to what he recollected, and that recollection can be aided by his notes and his typewritten reports. But we've had, I think, several witnesses who have diaries and notes that they used to refresh their recollection and have never been the subject of disclosure, although, we are certainly not opposed to providing those notes as we have them to both the Court and Defence counsel for use in determining the truth of these facts, and to determine the credibility of this witness's recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are prepared to turn over to the Defence and the Court those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Of course, we will not treat those notes as a statement, but they do have their probative value and a certain weight. Since the Prosecutor has those notes and the witness has authenticated them, I see no reason why the Defence shouldn't be given those notes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you have decided. So you will hand over to the Defence as soon as possible those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I believe we can do that today, probably later today. Or even now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think the Defence would need those notes right away, because they go on with the cross-examination and they may have to ask other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to say that as well. We would need them while the witness is still here, and we're dealing with names and not witness recollections. So very specific facts that were supplied by other persons. So we need those to determine whether we should ask some other questions in the cross-examination. We would be very grateful if we could receive them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I would suggest that you should now, please, hand over those notes to the Defence, as well as to the Court. And probably we should now suspend the cross-examination of this witness, because otherwise you can't use those notes in continuing in your cross-examination. We could probably bring in another witness while you -- maybe we can resume the cross-examination this afternoon so that you have the opportunity to go through the notes. Would this be acceptable to you, Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It's certainly acceptable to us, and I would -- I think the witness still has his copy of his notes, but if not, we should provide him a copy so he can also review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And I will, at this time, hand over -- it's a two-page document, and there is typing on both sides of both pages, so it's basically four pages in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that -- I mean, you may need the lunch break to go through it. So we can't resume the cross-examination before 2.00. Well, I'm sorry for the witness. You will have to stay and -- have you got a copy of your notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we can now move on to our next witness, and so if you don't mind, you will come back this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will go on with the cross-examination, and then re-examination and then probably a few questions from the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, perhaps this is right, before the witness is brought in, to do something, rather to comply with my duty. I have the certificates that I spoke about yesterday, and tendered them in English. I now have them in the original. These are the papers concerning the witness Sulejman Kavazovic. So may I ask the usher to take them and give them to the Court and to the Prosecution. I'm talking about those certificates of the post office that were addressed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. However, we can't admit them into evidence before the Prosecution has had the opportunity to go through those documents and check whether the translation is accurate. You can tender those documents, but we'll put off until, say, Friday, any decision about their admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Yes, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, let me deal with a few housekeeping matters. First of all, I wonder whether you have any comments on the draft decision on the visit to Ahmici, particular comments on the rules of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence does not Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. No comments. We will issue this decision. As you know, the visit is on unless there is an attack by NATO on Saturday, and we'll have to cancel it at the very last minute. Otherwise, we will go there on next Monday. Now, let me also say that we are, of course, grateful, as I said yesterday, to Counsel Pavkovic and all the other Defence counsel for telling us in advance of Friday of their wish to have a two-month break between the Prosecution and Defence case, and we should reciprocate by letting you know what we have decided. We think that it is in the best interests of justice and of an expeditious trial that we should not have such a long break but only a six-week break, so we would resume on the 30th of November and so have three weeks with the Defence case, three weeks before Christmas, and then we will continue in January, but by mid-February we should finish with this case, because really, it is otherwise -- we are very keen on a speedy trial. I think the Defence would -- should have not more than, say, seven to eight weeks for the Defence case? So -- now, the Prosecutor had 34 working days. There will be 37, probably. So roughly it's the equivalent of seven, eight weeks. Another piece of information that might be interesting and useful to you before the Pre-Defence conference, to be held on Friday, we have also decided about the order in which the various witnesses should be called by each Defence counsel, and we will follow the order of the indictees listed in the indictment. So first of all the witnesses for Zoran Kupreskic, then Mirjan and so on. So, Counsel Radovic, you will be the first one. It is more orderly and better organised if each counsel knows in advance when he will have to call his witness. Yes, please, Counsel Radovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the first place. I should merely like to say that my witnesses and my learned friend's witnesses are all combined. We shall have a number of joint witnesses, so you can put the two of us in one package so to speak. We should like to question our witnesses together. I mean, most of them. Especially those questions which relate to persecution. There are some questions which may perhaps refer solely to Mirjan, but most of our witnesses will testify in favour of both our accused. As I have already taken the floor, there will be very many witnesses but some of them shall be very brief. For instance, that tape which the Prosecution admitted -- I mean, [redacted] in the hospital, we ask the Prosecution to try to get the authentic tape so that we can really see the whole interview from beginning to end. We have not yet been answered that by the Prosecution, whether they can do it and it would be very important for us, because if we could see the whole tape then we would not need any witnesses who saw that particular programme in toto, and who know all that [redacted] said. So if we had precise information about that, perhaps we might give up some of the witnesses, refrain from calling some of the witnesses. Besides, we shall not be able to examine our witnesses as long as the Prosecution did, because we were not able to technically follow old examinations and old witnesses as the Prosecution were much worse (sic) equipped. We shall do our best to match the Prosecution but we simply don't have all these technical facilities at our disposal. But we should like to hear from the Prosecution if they could lay their hands on the whole tape, that is the tape of the whole programme. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and Mr. Radovic, we have not ignored that request to try to find the whole tape, and I anticipate that Mr. Tucker, will be here later this week, the investigator, will provide information about the whereabouts of that tape. I know that he has made efforts to locate an entire version, if there is an additional version to be had, and has made inquiries and can report on what he found when he testifies perhaps tomorrow or the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let me explain to you what is going on. We are now calling the Court witness that we mentioned yesterday, but we were told that because of a fire that broke out this morning in her hotel she was a bit under shock, but it's nothing to do with our hearing, so she will come here. We asked her to calm down. We have decided that somebody from the unit for protection of victims and witnesses should sit in court within sight so she feels a bit better, and then we will proceed. So in a few seconds or minutes she will be here. She will be witness CA. Yes, please. Good morning, Witness CA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you please stand and read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I -- I'm not literate. I can't read. Last time somebody read it for me and he translated, and I then repeated words after him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness CA, I'll read it to you and if you can just repeat, please. I will solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And nothing the but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We should go into closed session, because the witness requested we go into closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open Session)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just to announce a slight change in our remaining order, number 4, yes, will be testifying next, Your Honour. After number 4 we plan to put on number 7 because it involves the same kind of evidence, and we felt it would be more logical to put it in that record. Number 6, by the way, Your Honour, is -- can only testify on Thursday because of his commitments with the military. Then number 8 will be available virtually -- would be available tomorrow, or the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I was wondering whether we could try to finish by Thursday afternoon so that on Friday morning we could hold the pre-Defence conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We feel that would be very possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. So we could have the Friday afternoon off to prepare to go to Ahmici. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Will you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Could you state your identity, your full name to the Court and tell when you were born?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: My name is Stephen Hughes, and I was born on the 19th of March, 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were in Bosnia in 1993 as a member of the UNPROFOR. Could you tell the Court what your military career has been like?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: I started my military career in 1974, and retired recently in March 1998, serving 23 years and 6 months. The career has been varied, deployed to various areas around the world, and I have been or was promoted through the ranks to obtain my final rank of Warrant Officer Class 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you find yourself in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Between November 1992 to May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When were you stationed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: I was stationed in Vitez from November 1992 until late December 1992. We then moved to Tuzla, and then in February 1993 we came back to Vitez and remained there until we left Bosnia on May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us look at this period in the beginning of 1993. Could you tell the Court what your position was then within the BRITBAT and what your various missions were?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: My position at that time, I was battalion commander of 2 battalion, A company of the Cheshire Regiment, and our mission at that stage was to assist in the humanitarian aid that needed to be delivered to various locations within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I will first ask you to tell the Court what your recollection is of the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: My recollection of that date was the intensified fighting around the main Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On that day you were in Vitez; weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: On that day, we were tasked, yes, to enter into Vitez, due to the fact that there had been a large explosion, and I was tasked to go into the centre of Vitez to try and gain information to what the situation was within Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And on the basis of what you noticed, what was the situation within Vitez on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: The situation was that by moving around the area we formulated the opinion that the old town as we called the part of Vitez, was under attack from HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you able to notice any fighting among hostile military units, opposing military units?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Upon entering Vitez there was fire. We did notice -- or I noticed one wounded civilian crawling along the road. I then moved into the centre of Vitez to the area of the Vitez Hotel, moved south and then along the road moving west, and I noticed in the small built-up area a number of soldiers moving towards the old part of Vitez. These soldiers were moving in what we would call fire and manoeuvre. At this stage they didn't seem to be firing but were moving in an aggressive nature, again towards the old part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Those soldiers, which army did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Obviously from the direction they were moving and the direction they were moving in, it was recognised that they were HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you mentioned the old town of Vitez, do you have the Muslim part, the Muslim neighbourhood in mind?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. We call that the old part of Vitez, the Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On that day in Vitez did you notice any opposition to the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Not really. We quickly moved around and eventually I was placed in a static position near the mosque in old Vitez, and there I remained until we decided to try and evacuate as many people from the situation as we could. However, listening to the radio traffic, I could understand from other call-signs that they were trying to put themselves in positions to stop the attack on the old part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that time what did you think of what was happening in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: On assessing the situation, I would say that there was a concerted effort from the HVO to move and take over the old part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'd like us to move to the next day, the following day, the day -- the 17th of April, 1993. Is it right to say that on that day you went to Nadioci where the Bungalow or what is called the Swiss Cottage is to be found?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was tasked out that day to move into the area of the Bungalow, and also the area of Putis Jelinak. At this point I'd stopped on the road away from the area of the Bungalow, and I happened to be observing to the south, the high ground to the south of my position, when I noticed, or what I believed to be, an anti-aircraft weapon on the high ground. Initially it was difficult to be a hundred per cent sure it was an anti-tank -- or, I'm sorry, an anti-aircraft weapon. I tried looking through normal binoculars. Again, it didn't give me a hundred per cent that it was. At that stage I decided to traverse the turret on the vehicle and use the gunsight, which has a better magnification. Again, at this stage it became a little bit clearer, but I wouldn't say, again, is that stage that it was a hundred per cent, and there was still doubts. However, whilst observing, I saw people approach what I believed to be the anti-aircraft weapon which was situated on what I would call a flatbed trailer, a trailer with no sides. They mounted on to the anti-aircraft gun and fired between three to six rounds in what we would call the direct role towards the west. It was also at this stage that whilst observing the area, I noticed two men sat on the hillside observing towards the west. One had binoculars, and the other one, I believe, had a large radio. Whilst observing these two men, I heard what we call the report of either mortar or artillery being fired from behind the hill. Whilst observing, we then saw a vehicle move from the location of the anti-aircraft gun and move down the hill, and we tracked this as it came down. It eventually stopped at our location, and it was gestured to us that we should turn our gun away from pointing to the high ground where the position of the anti-aircraft gun was. We did this, and the jeep then proceeded down the road and returned to the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you be able to give us a summary description of that Bungalow? What did that Bungalow look like?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: From the outside, as you look at the Bungalow, it had a very steep roof. The roof looked as though it started from ground level and went straight up to an apex. At the base of the building was a small veranda, and halfway up the building looked to be a small balcony, and just above that looked again to be another small balcony. There was a very large door at the front. When you entered the Bungalow, on the left-hand side was a brick fireplace, an arched fireplace. In either the middle or to one side, I think to the right, was a table of some sort, which I believe at the time to have been a pool table. To the rear and left was a small bar area, and right at the rear were stairs leading up to the upper floors. The interior of the building was wood panelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could the usher show you Exhibit 119, P119? A building can be seen in the background. Is that the Bungalow you've just been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could the usher show you this document? There are no markings nor highlighting on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked P293.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, could you explain what this represents?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: This paperwork represents the radio log which is kept in the operations room, and it logs all radio traffic that is sent over the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And on the top left corner we have the date, haven't we? And then the times of radio traffic, as well as the call-signs of the various people who were intervening. What was your call-sign, your personal call-sign?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: My personal call-sign was Romeo Two Zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Does this document show that on that day you reported to your headquarters, to the Ops room, you reported what you had witnessed in Nadioci, what you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. The document actually states, in the text, the times that I called the Ops room and informed them of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us at what time you called the Ops room?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: The time was 15.39.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Just obviously further down is the second message, which again was transmitted at 16.09.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the aerial photograph which is behind you, are you able to localise the place where the Bungalow was built? Could you tell us where this anti-aircraft piece of ordinance was in this photograph? Maybe outside the field of this photograph, but where the anti-aircraft gun was?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: (Indicating). Up on the high ground, as it would be on the photograph itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So to the south, since, you know, it's upside down. The photograph is upside down. So it's south the place. Could you now tell us what this gun was targeting, what the target was?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: At that stage all I knew was that it was firing towards the west, but looking at the map and taking what we would call a ground appreciation from the map, which gave the gun limited arcs. It would fire -- if I could show you on the air photograph. (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, you are showing Lower Ahmici, which was targeting on either side of the main road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: (No audible response).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What were you able to see inside the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: When I went into the Bungalow with the ECMM monitor -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, let us first stick to the 17th of April, 1993. Did you go inside the Bungalow on that day?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: No, not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did you see on that day from outside the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: On that day, especially returning from the location I'd been observing from back to Vitez, the jeep that came down the hill was parked there, and also there was a number of HVO soldiers on the lower veranda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what uniforms they were in and what weapons they carried?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: The majority were in full camouflage uniform, both jacket and trousers. The majority, again, had AK-47 assault rifles, and I would say there were maybe one or two wearing black tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you go inside the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: I went inside the Bungalow with the ECMM monitor, and the -- I think the date was the 22nd. I may be wrong. Dates are difficult for me to remember, but we went in with that gentleman, an interpreter, and the HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What is your recollection of your going into the Bungalow? What did you see at that time?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: On entering the Bungalow, there was maybe 15 HVO soldiers. We entered the Bungalow. Both commanders, with the monitor, stood round a table and obviously were discussing the situation regarding the cease-fire. Again, we were in there for maybe 10, 15 minutes, and the situation changed drastically, which I believe at that stage cut short the meeting and we had to move outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And why did the situation change dramatically?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: One soldier came in. He seemed to be hysterical, waving a pistol around. At that time, not being next to the interpreter, the only indication that I got was that the majority of his anger was directed towards myself, and was -- the only word I could understand was UNPROFOR. I call the interpreter over, and he explained to me that this particular individual said that his family had been killed and that UNPROFOR had stood by and watched and done nothing about that. Again, at this stage, he left the building and went down to the second vehicle and tried to enter the second vehicle, which at that point had the BiH commanders in. At that stage he was finally restrained, taken away. Due to that situation, we all returned to the vehicles and then continued on with the tasks that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What is your recollection of the HVO commanders you saw on that day in the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: They obviously were discussing the positions which they had occupied, and no doubt were discussing the positions that were going to be visited that day by the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a very short clip of the video Exhibit P253 which has already been displayed to the judges. It lasts 10 to 15 seconds. And, witness, I shall ask you to have a close look at this short segment. I don't think that you've had the opportunity to see it before, and I shall ask you whether you can identify the location where this was taken, to start with, and then I'll ask you whether you are able to identify any of the people you may see in these pictures. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, were you able to identify the location where these pictures were taken, where this video was shot?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Looking at the video, and especially the interior, to me it would be the interior of the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you a hundred per cent sure, or is it just a hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: I would be a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You saw faces. Were you able to identify any of them?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: There was two people in the video that I recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you see them? When did you see these people?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: It would be difficult to say when it was that I'd seen these people, but, you know, their faces do stick in my mind. It is difficult to put a time, date and place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you be able to give a physical description of these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, the first one is fairly large build, he's chubby in the face, slightly receding hair, darkish skin. The second one I would say again was sort of medium height, again heavy sort of build, dark hair but bald on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Looking at the people here in this courtroom, would you be able to recognise either of these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: I can't see him. I can't see who is behind the pillar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why don't you stand and -- you can move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, you can move. You have to move, because indeed, this pillar is in your way.

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. No, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another day during your tour in Bosnia in the area of Vitez -- let us speak of the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could we have a break maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: For 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, you could us please tell the Court what happened on the 28th of April, 1993? You spent most of the day in Stari Vitez because there was a burial there, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. On that day the task given to me was to move into Stari Vitez and assist in the transfer of dead bodies between Stari Vitez and the school in Vitez. We met up and removed three bodies from the area of Stari Vitez. We also picked up a large vehicle and trailer, and from that point we escorted the party to the school inside Vitez itself. On arrival at the school, there was a vehicle already parked outside the school, which they proceeded to open the doors, which had already been loaded with a number of bodies wrapped in clear plastic bags. Again, it was at this stage then that the three bodies that were brought in from the area of Stari Vitez were taken into the school, and then the -- or they proceeded then to remove the bodies from the gymnasium within the school and place them onto the transport. At the time this was happening, an engineer vehicle, a light-wheel tractor, or bulldozer as it's commonly known, was in the Stari Vitez area preparing to dig a mass grave. Once the bodies had been loaded onto the transport, we then proceeded to escort the transport to the field and remain in location until the proceedings of burying the dead were complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it accurate to say that dead bodies of Croats were being swapped against Muslim bodies?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How many Croat bodies were there?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And how many Muslim bodies?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but it was put to me approximately 96.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And where were the Croat bodies, as it were, if I may use that expression, where were the bodies of former Croats? Where were they to be found?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: The one was found in a garage in, as I say, the Muslim area, or Stari Vitez, and the other two were actually brought out from the northern part of Stari Vitez, onto the main road where the lorry and trailer were waiting, and placed onto the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: They were not on the same location?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In respect of the bodies that were presented to you as being bodies of Muslims, do you know who had collected those bodies and where they came from?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: No. At that point there was no indication to us as who had collected the bodies and where exactly they'd come from. We only assumed, due to the situation, that the bodies had been collected from around the region of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, when you say "around Vitez", in your mind does that include Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that would include Ahmici. Within Vitez, over that period of time, the number of bodies that we did see was limited, but as you moved out of Vitez, going east, there were, again, a number of bodies lying on roadsides and in doorways of buildings. So we presumed from that that these bodies had been collected from the outlining villages which could include Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, could this exhibit be shown in this order? These are ten photographs. Could the usher help us? Your Honour, all these photographs were taken on the 28th of April, 1993 in Stari Vitez. They were taken by Mr. Penfound. This was will be confirmed by the witness. He was an officer in the British battalion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Whilst we're waiting for the first photograph to be shown, let me ask you this question: As going to be seen in these photographs, the bodies were wrapped in clear plastic bags. Were you, therefore, able to see whether they were soldiers who had been killed in combat or were there civilian bodies?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. Due to the nature of the way they were wrapped in the polythene bags, you could see by the clothing that I would say of all the bodies that I'd seen, which is, as I say, the 96, I only saw two that were wearing a camouflage jacket. The remainder were civilians, both male, female of varying age groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing bodies of babies, of children among those bodies?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: When we got to the field in Stari Vitez and they proceeded to initially lay the bodies on the grass prior to placing them into the grave, the purpose of this was so that they could try and identify who the body was. I saw two small, as you would say, packages or -- there were two small lying next -- or beginning of the line of bodies. I approached. You couldn't see into the plastic, because obviously the size of the package, it was obviously wrapped quite a few times. My initial thought was that it was children, but a local sort of gestured to me through body language, et cetera, that it was the heads from decapitated bodies. However, it couldn't be proved that that was the case. But I would say, you know, on reflection, that more than likely it was children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Among those bodies, bodies of Muslims, did you note bodies of elderly people?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. As I say, there was -- it covered all age groups. There were old, very old people, both male, female, teenagers, middle 20s, middle 30s. So it was a vast range of age groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you notice or did you get any clues as to the way these people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: The only clues that we had is that when the bodies were picked up is due to the fact that they were in plastic bags, that the large amounts of blood would go to the bottom of the bag, so, therefore, it would indicate to me that in that situation that they had died of some sort of gun-shot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On that location in Stari Vitez, this bulldozer of the BRITBAT dug two graves, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: (No audible answer)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How long did this operation, all the digging and all the burial ritual, how long did that take?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: The ritual of the burying took from, I would say, early afternoon through to early evening. Near the very end it was starting to get dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did -- were all the bodies buried in those graves identified with certainty?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, due to the fact that I was not involved in that detail, again I was there to offer assurance to the people carrying out that particular task, which were the Muslim people themselves, we were there, as I say, to protect them in case they come under any form of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please, usher, could you put the first photograph on the ELMO? Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I understood properly, the witness did not answer your question. He may not have understood your question the way you put it. You asked him whether they had been identified, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I'm going to put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether somebody was able to identify all of the bodies that were buried on that day?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: As far as I can answer, that there were a number of people and they were opening the bags, and as I could see it at that time, the bodies did have labels attached to them, which I believe was their identification. However, because I was not directly involved with the identification and the direct burying of the bodies, I can only surmise that there could have been people that were buried that day who were not able to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this first photograph and give us some comment, brief comment? Where was this photograph taken? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 303.

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. The picture that I'm looking at now was taken at the school in the middle of Vitez. It's the -- that particular vehicle was already in location when we arrived and had -- already had a number of bodies placed onto it. This photograph is indicating that they're continuing to fill the vehicle. This was the first vehicle to move off from the school to the field and be unloaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, this is the loading of the bodies which was then transported to Stari Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, most of the people who can be seen in this photograph are wearing masks. Why are they wearing masks?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Due to, again, the time of year, the weather, which the heat makes a big difference. It was the actual smell of the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you show the second photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 302.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell what this photograph shows and where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph shows the unloading of the first vehicle which we'd seen on the previous photograph, and this is taking place in the field in Stari Vitez where they initially lined the bodies up so that they could try and identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you show the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This is the operation which was to identify the bodies, as you stated before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. From what I could see from the procedures, again, as indicated within the photograph, is one individual would try to find the tag to identify the victim whilst, as you can again see in the photograph, another member wrote down the necessary details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In this photograph it can be seen -- what I'll call a bag was opened. Were the bags opened?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. In a lot of cases the bags were opened. Again, from earlier on, from what I could see, is that the individual bodies were actually tagged themselves. So the tag was actually inside fastened to the body or clothing and not fastened to the plastic bag.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 299.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this is a general view of the burial site; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can this bulldozer, the BRITBAT bulldozer, be seen in the photograph? I mean, the bulldozer that was used to dig the graves.

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. It can be seen to the left of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 298.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is this one of the graves dug by the BRITBAT vehicle?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are these the first bodies that were put into the grave?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: At that stage it looks to me that, yes, it's the first bodies to be placed into the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One can see that the plastic bags placed in this common grave are of various sizes. I see the second, starting from the bottom, it seems to be a very short bag. Do you remember that one in particular or other of similar sizes?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, I remember others of similar sizes. That could have been one that I had seen. Again, because of the smallness of the -- whether it's the body, as I say, it's wrapped so many times with the plastic that at that stage you couldn't see into it. And as I say, initially that's why I inquired to see if it was a small child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would that be that of a small child, or what could it have been?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: My assumption, eventually, is that -- though I was initially told that it was the head of a decapitated body, the package was too big for a head. So as I say, my later conclusion was that they were -- it was the body of a small child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 297.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So is this the same burial ceremony being carried on?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same burial ceremony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 296.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you want to make any comments on this photograph? This is the same common grave and the same operation?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: As I say, this went on for the remainder of the afternoon into early evening. By this stage, though we were still located at the field, we moved away from the proceedings, as we felt that it wasn't right for us to be looking on as sort of bystanders. So I made a decision to move my people away so that they could get on with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was there a Imam organising the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. Later on in the proceedings, as you look at the photograph, I would say they were more to the right, and there was a group who were praying and going through what are, you know, the procedures that they sort of go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were there a lot of people gathered on that site for the burial?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, there was quite a few people at the site, but I think that the overall control by the Muslims themselves, obviously they didn't want the whole place to be saturated, so again, I think they sort of controlled the situation so that the people that were there were there for the reasons of the proceedings rather than as onlookers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you notice that there were families present?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Not at that stage. As I say, we sort of stayed away from it and continued to observe mainly away from the burial site, due to the fact, again, I felt that, you know, we were there for the reason of observing out and giving them protection again because of the situation. They felt uneasy, that they could be sniped upon. So, as I say, our role was there just to be in the vicinity as a presence. So that was the decision I decided to take, is that we would move away and be seen to be doing the job that we were tasked to do that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can we see the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 295.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this is the same proceedings going on, being carried further; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was a long procedure, as I say, due to the fact that they first had to unload the bodies, line them out on the grass, identify, where possible, who they were before they could be placed in position in the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 294.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Does this photograph show the two parallel mass graves after they had been filled, of course?

utterances.speaker: Stephen Hughes
utterances.text: Yes. Initially one was dug. As soon as that was completed they carried on with a second, so eventually there was two mass graves dug on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall merely ask that Exhibits 293 to 3 -- wait a minute -- be tendered into evidence. I'll give you the numbers right now. 303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We were planning to go on until quarter past five. So, Mr. Pavkovic, could you tell us whether you have a lot of questions to ask of this witness? Do the Defence counsel plan to ask a lot of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, true, I do not know how many questions my colleagues will have, but my learned friend, Radovic, has already indicated that he would like to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Shall we have a start, Counsel Radovic? Shall we start now for 15 minutes and then we'll adjourn until tomorrow, or do you prefer to start tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'd rather if we started tomorrow morning if possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.30 then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 5.05 p.m. to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of October, 1998 at 9:30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
